new_statements.quote: Stress is characterized by the loudness of a particular syllable. There is a primary and a secondary stress in Subanon. [...] Primary stress is typically on the penultimate syllable in both unaffixed and affixed words. The maximum number of syllables in unaffixed words is four. [...] Following affixation, either by prefixation or suffixation, the primary stress shows consistency. It is always marked on the penultimate syllable. The secondary stress is only marked in words of four or more syllables. It falls on the alternate syllable of the syllable bearing the primary stress.
new_statements.citation: Estioca (Bulalang), Sharon Joy. 2020. A Grammar of Western Subanon. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa, sec. 2.2.2.3 'Stress'. [SISTER LANGUAGE Western Subanon [suc], Glottolog west2557 -- NOT Kolibugan Subanon itself]

new_statements.rule_in_words: In Western Subanon (the closest relative of Kolibugan, per Lobel 2013 and Estioca 2020) primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, including after prefixation or suffixation (stress shifts with the suffix: bóng.git > bong.gí.ton > bòng.gi.tá.nan); secondary stress on every other syllable leftward in words of 4+ syllables. No source opened says anything about stress in Kolibugan Subanon [skn] itself; the only Kolibugan-relevant remark is Lobel 2013 p. 287 fn. 3 that most Mindanao languages 'have lost contrastive stress'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Estioca 2020 p. 21: secondary stress marked only in words of four or more syllables, on the alternate syllable from the primary stress (e.g. kò.lom.bá.ngoy 'butterfly', bòng.gi.tá.nan 'fishhooks').
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Western Subanon ('typically', then 'always' penultimate). Not applicable to Kolibugan directly.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, elicited citation forms with affixation paradigms (Western Subanon of Malayal-Lintangan, Zamboanga). The statement is for the sister language; its applicability to Kolibugan Subanon is an inference only.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is for Western Subanon [suc] (Glottolog west2557; Siocon/Malayal Subanon), NOT for Kolibugan Subanon [skn] koli1253. Lobel 2013 (ch. 10) treats 'Western Kolibugan' as a distinct language grouped with Western Subanon in the 'Western Subanen' branch (Glottolog west2811, which is where koli1253 sits), and separately recognises 'Tawlet/Kalibugan' as a West-Nuclear Subanen language; 'Kolibugan/Kalibugan' is primarily an ethno-religious label for Islamised Subanen (Christie 1909; Lobel 2013), so the ISO code skn does not map cleanly onto one of Lobel's varieties. hh.bib's note on Abingosa 2020 ('Kolibugan here is Western Subanon, pc Bill Hall via Jason Lobel') shows the same ambiguity. Estioca 2020 p. 4 calls Western Kolibugan 'the closest cousin of Subanon'.

[...] Primary stress is typically on the penultimate syllable in both unaffixed and affixed words. The maximum number of syllables in unaffixed words is four. sources.locator: p. 21 (PDF p. 48), sec. 2.2.2.3; examples (3a-c) same page
sources.note: SISTER LANGUAGE, Western Subanon [suc] = west2557, not Kolibugan. Sec. 2.2.2.3 'Stress', p. 21 (PDF p. 48): primary stress is on the penultimate syllable in unaffixed and affixed words (shifts rightward under suffixation), secondary stress on alternating syllables in words of four or more syllables. p. 4 (PDF p. 31): 'Some Subanons can also understand Western Kolibugan, the closest cousin of Subanon of the other six Subanen languages (Lobel 2013).' Nothing said about Kolibugan stress.

sources.citation: Lobel, Jason William. 2013. Philippine and North Bornean languages: issues in description, subgrouping, and reconstruction. PhD diss., University of Hawai'i at Manoa. Ch. 10 'Subanen Reconstructions', pp. 303-358.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Ch. 10 is based on Lobel's own 2006-2011 fieldwork on all eight Subanen languages incl. 'Western Kolibugan' and 'Tawlet/Kalibugan', but is purely historical-comparative (sound changes, subgrouping, 618 Proto-Subanen reconstructions); it contains no stress or accent statement for any Subanen language. The only relevant remark is general: p. 287 fn. 3 (PDF p. 305) 'It is also worth noting that most languages native to Mindanao and areas further south have lost contrastive stress.'

sources.note: Ethnography with word-lists (Appendix I, p. 107 ff; hh.bib tags the Nueva Reus/Zamboanga list as 'likely Kolibugan Subanon [skn]'). The orthography note before the word-lists covers only vowel and consonant values; no accent marks and no statement on stress. Kalibugan appear only as Islamised Subanun settlements (ethnographic remarks).
